tagline.text: A Taoist temple to the sea goddess Mazu above San Fernando Bay

location.label: Location
location.text: Ma-Cho Temple Driveway, Barangay II, San Fernando City, La Union

duration.label: Time needed

children.text: Ma-Cho Temple is a Taoist temple on a hill north of San Fernando, La Union, overlooking San Fernando Bay and dedicated to the sea goddess Mazu. Built in the 1970s by Chinese-Filipino devotees and opened in 1978, it is known for its five-door pailou gate, drum and bell towers, a wooden dome and a scenic terrace.

Ma-Cho Temple sits on a headland at the northern edge of San Fernando, the capital of La Union, jutting out toward the sea. The address is Ma-Cho Temple Driveway in Barangay II, and the view takes in San Fernando Bay and the sea to the west. One visitor reported a drive of about three and a half hours from Manila, and it is close enough to the town center to reach on foot. The name Ma-Cho refers to Mazu (Tianhou), the Chinese sea goddess, and the Chinese name of the temple is 菲律濱隆天宮.

Mazu is the deified form of a woman named Lin Moniang, said to have been born around 960 in Fujian, and she is worshipped as a protector of seafarers who rescued fishermen from storms. In the Philippines there is a distinctive belief that she is the same figure as Our Lady of Caysasay of Taal, Batangas. According to the temple's own account, Taiwanese fishermen sent the Mazu image in gratitude for shelter from a typhoon, though sources disagree on the year, giving 1968 and 1972. Either way, it is clear that this temple is a place where the Chinese-Filipino community and local Catholic faith overlap.
Groundbreaking took place on
September 11, 1975
, and the main construction began on December 2, 1976. The Mazu image was enshrined on July 3, 1978, and the temple was inaugurated on
December 6, 1978

. Construction was led by the Chinese-Filipino devotee Dy Keh Hio and designed by the architect Thomas Diokno. Some descriptions call it one of the largest Taoist temples in the Philippines. Wikipedia reports that Taiwanese craftsmen took part in the building. The site covers about 9,000 square meters and sits on a hill about 21 meters (70 feet) high, so you climb gradually through stairs and courtyards from the entrance to the main hall. Devotees offer incense, food and money at the altar and make their wishes.

Ma-Cho Temple is not only for the faithful; it is an open temple that anyone, including Catholics and tourists, can enter and look around. Around the fifth day of the eighth lunar month each year, the Mazu image makes a pilgrimage to the Basilica of St. Martin of Tours in Taal, Batangas, and returns, and the festival held then is the temple's biggest event. On ordinary days, the best way to visit is to walk through the gently incense-scented gardens and climb in order through the stairs, towers and the viewing terrace. The fact that the Mazu image travels all the way to Taal every year makes this temple unique to the Philippines.

At the entrance stands a large pailou gate with five doorways. Its design is described as derived from Indian originals, and it is the temple's first photo spot. Passing through this gate into the courtyard, you enter the temple grounds.

In the middle of the circular brick courtyard is a pond with water lilies and goldfish, and another pond has a small pagoda standing in it. On one side stand animal statues considered good luck charms, and there is a small structure for burning offerings. A shrine to the earth god Tho Ti Kong is also on the grounds, so you can see other deities as well.

blocks.title: Main hall with drum and bell towers

children.text: The main hall is described as seven stories and eleven tiers, with a Drum Tower on the left and a Bell Tower on the right. Inside is a large open space, with the altar set behind reflective glass. Craftsmen from Taiwan are said to have taken part in the decoration and woodwork, and camphor wood is said to have been used for the carved lions and dragons.

The dome inside the main hall is described as having layered tiers of wood carved with saints that interlock with one another. When you look up, it is the most striking decoration. The temple brochure says there are 13 tiers of wood carvings.

The Mazu image on the altar is a small wooden figure about 20 centimeters (8 inches) tall, wearing a Chinese-style headdress and robe, with eyes closed and hands clasped at the chest. It sits behind glass, so it is hard to see when it is crowded.

The upper terrace beside the main hall has a statue of Guanyin and an eight-sided pavilion. The sea view opens wide, making it the best spot for scenery in the temple. Vehicles can drive up beside or behind the main hall, so anyone who finds the stairs difficult can use that route.

Eighteen Arhats line the terrace retaining wall, and below the main hall is a meditation room with red kneelers. The entrance wall is carved with stone statues of the 18 saints. These stone statues on the entrance wall are described as carved from imported stone.

blocks.title: Guardian lions and the Buyong ritual

children.text: Two guardian lions stand on the main hall steps: the male has a ribbon strung with coins, and the female holds a cub. In the weekly Buyong session, devotees reportedly communicate with the gods. The session is described as a ritual in which a priest-like leader reads Mazu's message to the devotees. Offerings are placed on the table in front of the altar.

items.title: 1–2 hour temple route
items.subtitle: From the pailou to the terrace

children.text: Pass through the pailou at the driveway and enter the courtyard. Take your time looking at the ponds and animal statues, and take photos.
Climb the stairs into the main hall to see the altar, the wooden dome and the Mazu image. If devotees are praying, keep a quiet distance.
Walk around the drum and bell towers and look into the meditation room below the main hall.
Climb to the upper terrace to see the Guanyin statue, the octagonal pavilion and the 18 Arhats, and enjoy the view of San Fernando Bay.
Come back down, look at the stone statues of the 18 saints on the entrance wall, and leave the temple.
The Pindangan Ruins are said to be on the way to the temple, so if you have time, stop by them as well.
The dress code is strict, so check your clothing before you reach the entrance.
See Ma-Cho Temple first. Mornings are cooler and the temple is quieter.
Come down to town to see the area around the city hall plaza and the cathedral, and walk through San Fernando's historic district.
Have lunch at a restaurant in town or a cafe on the coast.
Head to the beach to the south and enjoy surfing or a beach walk at San Juan.
Watch the sunset and return to Manila or Baguio.
Agoo Basilica is about 33km south, and many people combine the two in one day.

Take a long-distance bus toward the Ilocos region from Manila and get off in San Fernando town. The temple is fairly close to the center, so you can take a tricycle from the city hall plaza. Tell the driver in advance to drop you in front of the temple driveway.
By car, use NLEX, SCTEX and TPLEX to reach the La Union coastal highway. One traveler reported about three and a half hours from Manila, but this depends on traffic.
Bus companies, fares and departure times change, so confirm locally.
From Clark International Airport (CRK), take TPLEX north to reach La Union. Flights change by season, so check airline announcements.
One traveler reported about 2 hours coming down the mountain from Baguio by Naguilian Road or another route. Kennon Road is often restricted or closed, so check road advisories.
By bus, take one bound for San Fernando from Otek Street in Baguio, then continue by tricycle.
From San Fernando town, a tricycle is convenient to reach the temple. Vehicles can drive up beside or behind the main hall, while the front can only be reached by stairs from below.
La Union has its dry season from November to May, which makes the outdoor stairs and terrace of the temple comfortable to walk. The midday sun is strong, so morning or late afternoon is recommended.

During the Mazu festival on September 21–26, the image returns from the Basilica of St. Martin of Tours in Taal, and a procession through San Fernando's business district, a dragon dance and other cultural performances are said to take place. The schedule can change every year, so check with the city tourism office or the temple's announcements.

Around Ma-Cho Temple there are only a few food stalls, and meals and lodging are mostly in San Fernando town or along the San Juan beachfront. San Juan, a surf town, has many cafes and places to stay, which makes it a good place to combine into one trip and spend a night. A temple visit usually takes 1–2 hours, so the rest of your time is best spent in town and by the sea.
In La Union you can try Ilocano food and seafood. Restaurants often close or move, so check the latest ratings and opening status before you go.
Visitors report a strict dress code. Avoid short skirts, short pants, sleeveless tops, spaghetti-strap tops, see-through clothing, and anything that leaves the shoulders or back bare.
Take off your hat indoors. Shoes are said to be allowed inside.
Pets are said not to be allowed.
The temple's official website (machotemple.org) lists daily hours of 7 AM to 5 PM and a 2024 travel guide agrees, but some sources say 24 hours, so hours may change; check before you go.
The viewing terrace involves going up and down stairs, so comfortable shoes are best.
Do not take close-up photos of devotees praying or of rituals without permission.
During the September festival, arrive early and keep your valuables in front of you.
The temple's official website is machotemple.org, and a Facebook group is also said to be active. Check there, and by phone, for opening hours and event schedules.
Photos of the sea view come out cleanest on a clear morning. To avoid backlight, shoot from the terrace looking toward the sea.
The temple is a place of worship where devotees light incense and pray. Do not walk in front of people who are praying or make loud noise.
The dress code differs between sources and opening hours may change, so check local announcements.
The front entrance can only be reached by stairs, so if walking is hard for you, use the side or rear road that vehicles take up.
In typhoons and heavy rain, the coastal road and the temple stairs can be slippery.
During the festival, roads and parking are very crowded and pickpockets become more common.
Do not use flash in front of the altar and the statues when taking photos.
The provincial capital of La Union, where the temple stands, is close to the city hall plaza, the cathedral and the coast. It makes a good combination with the temple in one trip.
A surf town close to San Fernando with many cafes and places to stay, good for a rest after seeing the temple.
A waterfall in inland La Union that is a candidate to combine with a temple trip. Access and weather need to be confirmed locally.
A historic town in Batangas that enshrines Our Lady of Caysasay, regarded as the same figure as Mazu. It is the place the Mazu image visits on its pilgrimage during the annual festival.
